name: Aaron Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the customer insights team at the head office of a big supermarket chain, six analysts on the fourth floor. We look at loyalty-card data and tell the buying teams things like why oat milk sales dropped in the north. I start with coffee and a dashboard check, then it's meetings, then I spend the afternoon rewriting slides my team made so the category directors will actually read them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzles, and I like that I get to try every new tool first, I've got about five AI assistants open most days. What wears me out is that I'm still not great at the people side. I promoted fast because I was good with data, and now I spend half my week managing feelings, which nobody trained me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, the tools are useful but they were oversold. I'd probably post something nerdy about which bits actually worked. At work I'd keep using them, because they genuinely save me an hour or two a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay pretty good. My job's secure, the team stays six people, and I keep being the guy who knows the tools. The only pressure is the normal one of proving I deserve the promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep building little AI shortcuts for the team, like an automatic summary of the weekly sales numbers. I'd ask for the data-leadership course the company runs in spring. And I'd keep putting money aside for a deposit, about 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat even. Part of me would be disappointed, because I find this stuff exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed? Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think the tools could take the boring bits away from my team. My analysts spend Monday mornings copying numbers into slides, and I'd love a world where nobody does that again. If it all stalls, they keep doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would be happiest if it stalled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Bogdan, who's been there twelve years and doesn't trust anything he didn't build in a spreadsheet himself. He'd be smug for a month. I'd let him have it, he's earned it.

say: The tools are **useful but oversold**, and I'd post about which bits actually worked.
At work I'd **keep using them** because they save me an hour or two daily.
think: My **job stays secure** and the team stays at six analysts.
My only real pressure is **proving the promotion** was deserved.
do: Build **small AI shortcuts** for the team, like an automatic weekly sales summary.
Ask for the company's **data-leadership course** in spring.
Keep saving **300 a month** towards a flat deposit.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **disappointment** that the boring work doesn't go away.
S0.quote: My analysts spend Monday mornings copying numbers into slides, and I'd love a world where nobody does that again.
fieldNote: He is the rare person **disappointed** by the hype fading, because he likes the tools.
His instinct is to use AI to **remove drudgery** for his analysts, not to cut them.
He admits his weak spot is the **people side** of managing.

steps.text: Build an automatic weekly sales summary for the team
Sign up for the spring data-leadership course
Save 300 a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to share the gains, a four-day week, not four fewer analysts. I'd say it in the staff forum and probably get a slightly awkward look from my director. Online I'd be the guy posting long threads about productivity and who gets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, maybe better than fine, because I'm the one who knows how to run the tools. But I'd be lying if I said my team was safe. Insights work is writing, checking and summarising, so I'd expect the company to ask why it needs six analysts when two and a good system will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my director in the first month with a plan that keeps people but changes their jobs, so analysts spend more time with stores and shoppers and less time on slides. I'd train every analyst on the tools myself, one afternoon a week. I'd also look outside, quietly, at AI product roles in retail tech firms, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly on behalf of the team. I feel guilty that the thing I'm excited about is the thing that might cut them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your director said, thanks, but we're cutting two analysts anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fight for redeployment first, there are always gaps in store operations and supply planning. If my director still cut two analysts, I'd make sure it wasn't Bogdan just because he's the slowest with the new tools. Twelve years of knowing why the numbers look weird is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look outside. Isn't that a bit at odds with fighting for the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is, and I've thought about that. I think I can do both for a while. I'd stay as long as I can actually protect people, and if I can't, there's no point me staying just to manage the cuts.

say: The company should **share the gains** with a four-day week, not fewer analysts.
I'd say that in the **staff forum** and post long threads about productivity online.
think: I'm probably fine because **I run the tools**, but my team isn't safe.
Insights work is **writing and summarising**, so two analysts plus software could replace six.
do: Pitch my director a plan to move analysts toward **store and shopper work**.
Train every analyst on the tools myself, **one afternoon** a week.
Look quietly at **AI product roles** in retail tech firms.
feel: **Uneasy** for the team and **guilty** that his excitement could cost them jobs.
S1.quote: If my director still cut two analysts, I'd make sure it wasn't Bogdan just because he's the slowest with the new tools.
fieldNote: His own position looks **secure**, but he worries about his team's.
He frames a **four-day week** as the fair way to share the productivity gains.
He is open about the **contradiction** between fighting for the team and job hunting.

steps.text: Run a weekly afternoon training analysts on the AI tools
Raise a four-day week proposal in the staff forum
Apply for AI product roles at retail tech firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, fast: taxes on the companies that gain, money for people who lose, and some say for workers in how it's rolled out. I'd probably join whatever campaign springs up. At work I'd tell my team straight that I don't know what happens, rather than pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm gone too, just a bit later than the analysts. If the AI does almost any thinking work as well as a person, a junior manager of a data team is the easiest role to cut. Being good with tools doesn't help when the tool doesn't need a person to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for a deposit and keep the money liquid, about five months' worth, in case I'm out of work. I'd spend the two years before it arrives building something hands-on alongside my job, maybe learning to fix bikes properly with my friend who runs a repair workshop, since robots don't come until 2031. And I'd join a campaign group pushing for an income guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's strange, because I'm the person who loved this stuff, and now it's the thing I'd lose my job to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was a nurse and my dad drove delivery vans, and they were so proud when I got a desk job with a title. My parents worked hard so I'd never have to do hands-on work, and I'd be telling them I want to learn to fix bikes. I think Dad would laugh and then quietly help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is bike repair really a plan, or a comfort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more comfort than plan, if I'm honest. It's three extra years, not a career. But I'd rather have some practical skill and three years of breathing room than nothing at all.

say: We need **emergency rules**: taxes on the winners and money for those who lose.
I'd **join a campaign** and tell my team honestly that I don't know what happens.
think: A **junior data manager** is one of the easiest roles to cut once AI can think.
Being good with tools doesn't help when the tool **needs no person**.
do: Stop deposit saving and keep about **five months** of money ready.
Learn **bike repair** at a friend's workshop for three extra years of breathing room.
Join a **campaign group** pushing for an income guarantee.
feel: **Alarmed**, and thrown by losing his job to the technology he loved.
S2.quote: My parents worked hard so I'd never have to do hands-on work, and I'd be telling them I want to learn to fix bikes.
fieldNote: The early adopter sees no **protection** in his skills once AI matches people.
His hands-on fallback is honest: he calls it **more comfort** than a real plan.
His **parents' pride** in his desk job makes the change feel personal.

steps.text: Pause deposit saving and keep five months of cash ready
Learn bike repair at a friend's workshop on weekends
Join a campaign group pushing for an income guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this well if we start now, and I'd push hard for that. I'd want the company to publish a plan for its staff by next year. Online I'd keep posting, but more about solutions than doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get three, maybe four good years as a manager, and the experience would help me move somewhere else. By 2031 the office side is gone for most people like me. The extra time matters because I could actually switch into something I'd want to do, instead of grabbing whatever's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask to move into the store operations team, where you're closer to real shops and real people, and the hands-on side lasts till 2034. I'd keep building savings to six months. I'd use the AI every day to get faster at my current job while I still have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but energised too. I like having a problem to solve, even if it's my own life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would store operations give you that insights doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time in the actual stores, with managers, staff, deliveries, all the stuff a system can't see from a dashboard. I'd rather learn how a supermarket actually runs than be the last data guy explaining why oat milk dropped. It also puts me next to the people who'll still be there longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your team in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them about the store ops route too and help anyone who wants it. Some will retire, some will move. I'd want to look back and know I gave them the warning I had.

say: Five years is enough to **do this well** if the company publishes a plan soon.
I'd post more about **solutions than doom** online.
think: I'd get **three or four** good years before office work goes for people like me.
Extra time lets me **choose a switch** I want, not grab whatever is left.
do: Ask to move into **store operations**, closer to shops, staff and deliveries.
Build savings to **six months** of expenses.
Use AI daily to get **faster at my job** while I still have it.
feel: **Anxious** but energised, treating his own career as a **problem to solve**.
S3.quote: I'd rather learn how a supermarket actually runs than be the last data guy explaining why oat milk dropped.
fieldNote: He uses the time to move toward **hands-on retail** work that lasts until 2034.
He wants to pass on the **same warning** to his team that he has.
His **energy** returns with five years, unlike the fast picture.

steps.text: Apply for an internal move into store operations
Build savings up to six months of expenses
Use AI daily to speed up current analysis work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and the worst thing would be wasting it. I'd push for the company to fund retraining for anyone who wants it. Online I'd probably start writing about how to plan a career around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd have most of my thirties to build something. I think the end point still takes my office job, so I'd use the time to get into a role that mixes people and physical places, maybe running stores or a distribution centre. That would carry me to around 2039, and by then I'd hope the world has some answer for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in insights for two or three years, learn everything I can, then move into store management. I'd start a part-time course in retail operations. I'd also go back to saving for a flat, because ten years is long enough to need somewhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but a lot lighter. It feels like a long project rather than an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust governments to use the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. They're bad at long things. I'd plan my own life as if the government does nothing, and campaign as if it might do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new analyst joining your team today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, but also learn the business, the stores, the suppliers. The person who knows why things happen in the real world lasts longer than the person who just makes the charts. I wish someone had told me that at twenty-two.

say: Ten years is a **real chance**, and wasting it would be the worst outcome.
I'd push for **company-funded retraining** and write about career planning online.
think: The end point still takes my **office job**, so I'd shift into stores or distribution.
That role could carry me to **around 2039**, buying most of my thirties.
do: Stay in insights **two or three years** to learn as much as possible.
Start a **part-time course** in retail operations.
Go back to **saving for a flat**.
feel: Still **anxious**, but it feels like a long project, not an emergency.
S4.quote: I'd plan my own life as if the government does nothing, and campaign as if it might do something.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose his office job** but has time to build a path.
He separates **personal planning** from political hope, trusting neither government nor luck.
His advice to juniors stresses **knowing the business**, not just the tools.

steps.text: Start a part-time retail operations course
Restart saving for a flat deposit each month
Campaign for company-funded retraining for all staff

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the job and the thing I'm good at in the same moment, with no time to build anything else. What would help is a guaranteed income floor, and a company that tells us honestly what's coming, early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like to be excited and scared about the same thing. I've spent three years being the guy who brings AI into meetings, and in the fast picture I'm basically handing it my own job.

headlineQuote: I've spent three years being the guy who brings AI into meetings, and in the fast picture I'm basically handing it my own job.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old manager** of six analysts in customer insights at a supermarket head office.
He uses **AI tools daily** and loves them, but leans left and wants gains shared with workers.
He has about **five months** of savings and is saving for a flat deposit.
He feels **calm** in the plateau, but alarmed by fast AGI, which would take the job he built on tools.
With more time he plans a move into **store operations**, closer to physical retail work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose his job and his main skill at once.
whatWouldHelp: A company that tells staff **honestly and early** what is coming.
